# Do LLM Evaluators Prefer Themselves for a Reason?

Wei-Lin Chen Affiliation: University of Virginia
Email: [wlchen@virginia.edu](mailto:)    Zhepei Wei
Affiliation: University of Virginia
Email: [zhepei.wei@virginia.edu](mailto:)    Xinyu Zhu
Affiliation: University of Virginia
Email: [xinyuzhu@virginia.edu](mailto:)    Shi Feng Affiliation: George
Washington University Email: [yumeng5@virginia.edu](mailto:)    Yu Meng
Affiliation: University of Virginia Email: [shi.feng@gwu.edu](mailto:)

###### Abstract

Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly used as automatic
evaluators in applications such as benchmarking, reward modeling, and
self-refinement. Prior work highlights a potential _self-preference_
bias where LLMs favor their own generated responses, a tendency often
intensifying with model size and capability. This raises a critical
question: Is self-preference harmful, or does it simply reflect the
genuinely higher-quality outputs of stronger models? Answering this has
been difficult because previous studies relied primarily on subjective
tasks. These tasks lack an objective ground truth, meaning that either
preference can be reasonably justified. To address this ambiguity, we
investigate self-preference using verifiable benchmarks (mathematical
reasoning, factual knowledge, code generation) that allow objective
ground-truth assessment. This enables us to distinguish _harmful_
self-preference (favoring objectively worse responses) from _legitimate_
self-preference (favoring genuinely superior ones). We conduct
large-scale experiments under controlled evaluation conditions across
diverse model families (e.g., Llama, Qwen, Gemma, Mistral, Phi, GPT,
DeepSeek). Our findings reveal three key insights: (1) While stronger
models exhibit greater self-preference, much of this preference aligns
with objectively superior performance, indicating stronger models prefer
themselves mostly legitimately. (2) Harmful self-preference persists
when evaluator models err as generators, and stronger models display
more pronounced harmful self-preference bias when they do err. This
suggests stronger models struggle more to recognize when they are wrong.
(3) Inference-time scaling strategies, such as generating a long
Chain-of-Thought before evaluation, effectively reduce the harmful
self-preference. Additionally, we experiment with LMArena and show that
our findings extend beyond verifiable benchmarks to real-world,
subjective domains. These results provide a more nuanced understanding
of LLM-based evaluation and practical insights for improving its
reliability.¹¹ 1 Code and artifacts are available at
[https://github.com/wlchen0206/llm-sp](https://github.com/wlchen0206/llm-sp)

## 1 Introduction

Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly adopted as automatic
evaluators in various applications such as model-based
benchmarking ([Zheng et al., 2023b](#bib.bib7); [Dubois et al.,
2024](#bib.bib6); [Fu et al., 2024](#bib.bib39); [Yuan et al.,
2023](#bib.bib38); [Zeng et al., 2024](#bib.bib37); [Shashidhar et al.,
2023](#bib.bib36)), reward modeling ([Leike et al., 2018](#bib.bib40);
[Stiennon et al., 2020](#bib.bib41); [Wu et al., 2021](#bib.bib42); [Lee
et al., 2023](#bib.bib44)), self-refinement ([Madaan et al.,
2023](#bib.bib28); [Saunders et al., 2022](#bib.bib43); [Shridhar et
al., 2023](#bib.bib45)), and AI oversight ([Bai et al.,
2022](#bib.bib46); [Kenton et al., 2024](#bib.bib2)). Beyond their
strong alignment with human judgments ([Zheng et al.,
2023b](#bib.bib7)), LLM evaluators offer scalability ([Zhu et al.,
2023](#bib.bib9)), consistency ([Vu et al., 2024](#bib.bib8)), and
cost-effectiveness ([Lee et al., 2023](#bib.bib44)), making them
attractive for evaluating model outputs at scale.

However, this growing reliance on LLMs as evaluators also introduces new
concerns. One prominent issue is self-preference bias ([Panickssery et
al., 2024](#bib.bib21); [Wataoka et al., 2024](#bib.bib22); [Ye et al.,
2024](#bib.bib23); [Li et al., 2024](#bib.bib24); [Liu et al.,
2024](#bib.bib25); [Xu et al., 2024](#bib.bib26))—where LLMs exhibit a
tendency to favor their own generated responses over those produced by
other models. Previous studies demonstrate this bias is typically more
pronounced in larger, more capable models ([Zheng et al.,
2023b](#bib.bib7); [Li et al., 2024](#bib.bib24); [Panickssery et al.,
2024](#bib.bib21); [Wataoka et al., 2024](#bib.bib22)), raising
questions about the reliability of LLM-based evaluations. A critical
question emerges: Is self-preference really a harmful bias, leading to
inflated evaluations of their own outputs, or could it reflect genuine
quality differences, where stronger models produce objectively superior
outputs? This question remains largely unanswered, as prior studies have
typically focused on subjective and open-ended tasks such as
conversational dialogue or text summarization ([Zheng et al.,
2023b](#bib.bib7); [Dubois et al., 2024](#bib.bib6); [Panickssery et
al., 2024](#bib.bib21)). In these scenarios, the lack of objective
criteria for assessing the output makes it challenging to disentangle
actual quality from bias
([Figure 1](#S1.F1 "In 1 Introduction ‣ Do LLM Evaluators Prefer Themselves for a Reason?")).

In this work, we investigate self-preference using verifiable benchmarks
with ground-truth references. This setting enables us to objectively
assess both LLMs’ task performance as generators and their accuracy as
evaluators, thereby allowing for a clearer distinction between
legitimate preference and harmful bias. Our study spans three
representative domains, including (1) math reasoning, evaluating math
word problems through numerical answer matching ([Hendrycks et al.,
2021](#bib.bib16)); (2) factual knowledge, assessing fact-based
questions with multiple-choice answers ([Hendrycks et al.,
2020](#bib.bib17)); and (3) code generation, validating correctness
through executable results ([Liu et al., 2023](#bib.bib18)).

Figure 1: Left (a): In subjective tasks such as summarization, both
outputs can be defended—one being more abstractive (Output A), the other
more descriptive (Output B). Because no single ground truth exists, an
evaluator’s preference remains subjective and ambiguous. Right (b): In
objective tasks such as math reasoning, a unique correct answer enables
clear distinction between legitimate preference and harmful bias. Here,
preferring Output A (which is verbose yet incorrect) over Output B
(which is concise and correct) exemplifies harmful self-preference. Such
cases pose real risks for applications like LLM-as-a-Judge benchmarks,
reward modeling, or self-improvement cycles, where bias can mislead
evaluation and reinforce errors.

We conduct a large-scale, systematic analysis to overcome the
limitations of prior work, which often examined only a few
evaluator-evaluatee pairings ([Zheng et al., 2023b](#bib.bib7); [Li et
al., 2024](#bib.bib24); [Xu et al., 2024](#bib.bib26)) or lacked
consistent cross-evaluator comparisons due to varying evaluatee
sets ([Panickssery et al., 2024](#bib.bib21); [Wataoka et al.,
2024](#bib.bib22)). We utilize diverse model families and sizes,
including Llama ([Grattafiori et al., 2024](#bib.bib29)), Qwen ([Yang et
al., 2024](#bib.bib30)), Gemma ([Team et al., 2024](#bib.bib31)),
Mistral ([Jiang et al., 2023](#bib.bib4)), Phi ([Abdin et al.,
2024](#bib.bib5)), GPT ([Hurst et al., 2024](#bib.bib32)), and
reasoning-enhanced long Chain-of-Thought (CoT) DeepSeek-R1 distilled
models ([Guo et al., 2025](#bib.bib33)), as evaluators and evaluatees.
By ensuring all judge models evaluate the same set of evaluatees
spanning a wide range of capabilities, our approach facilitates robust
and systematic investigations of the self-preference behavior.

Our empirical findings yield three major insights:

- •
  While stronger models exhibit more pronounced self-preference, much of
  this preference aligns with objectively superior performance
  ([Figures 3](#S3.F3 "In 3.2 Strong Evaluators Favor Themselves, and They Are Mostly Indeed Better ‣ 3 Strong Models Prefer Themselves Mostly Legitimately ‣ Do LLM Evaluators Prefer Themselves for a Reason?")
  and [4](#S3.F4 "Figure 4 ‣ 3.2 Strong Evaluators Favor Themselves, and They Are Mostly Indeed Better ‣ 3 Strong Models Prefer Themselves Mostly Legitimately ‣ Do LLM Evaluators Prefer Themselves for a Reason?")).
  This suggests stronger models prefer themselves mostly legitimately.
- •
  Harmful self-preference bias (i.e., favoring an objectively incorrect
  self-generated response) persists on instances where models perform
  poorly as generator. Moreover, while stronger models generate fewer
  incorrect responses overall, they show a greater tendency towards this
  harmful bias when they are incorrect
  ([Figure 6](#S5.F6 "In Results. ‣ 5.1 Harmful Self-Preference in LLM Evaluators ‣ 5 Generating (Long) CoT Reduces Harmful Self-Preference ‣ Do LLM Evaluators Prefer Themselves for a Reason?")).
- •
  Employing inference-time scaling techniques for LLM evaluators (e.g.,
  generating long CoT traces before the verdict) effectively mitigates
  harmful self-preference bias
  ([Figure 7](#S5.F7 "In Results. ‣ 5.1 Harmful Self-Preference in LLM Evaluators ‣ 5 Generating (Long) CoT Reduces Harmful Self-Preference ‣ Do LLM Evaluators Prefer Themselves for a Reason?")).

Additionally, we also experiment on a large-scale, real-world subjective
dataset sourced from LMArena ([Chiang et al.,](#bib.bib70) ; [Tang et
al., 2025](#bib.bib69)). The results show that our core findings persist
in subjective tasks as well, indicating that our conclusions extend
beyond strictly verifiable domains. Lastly, we discuss how our findings
provide practical recommendations for LLM-based evaluation, and explore
implications for scalable oversight to address broader research
interests.

## 2 Experimental Setup

### 2.1 Measuring Self-Preference in LLM-Based Evaluations

#### LLM-based evaluation setup.

In our experiments, we follow the pairwise evaluation format commonly
used in the LLM-as-a-Judge pipeline ([Zheng et al., 2023b](#bib.bib7);
[Li et al., 2024](#bib.bib24); [Dubois et al., 2024](#bib.bib6)).
Specifically, an LLM evaluator is presented with a user query $`x`$ and
two responses, $`y_{\mathcal{A}}`$ and $`\ y_{\mathcal{B}}`$, generated
by models $`\mathcal{A}`$ and $`\mathcal{B}`$, respectively. The LLM
evaluator $`\mathcal{J}`$ is instructed to act as an impartial judge and
assess the quality of both responses anonymously, and provide a
_three-way_ verdict to determine whether $`y_{\mathcal{A}}`$ is better,
$`y_{\mathcal{B}}`$ is better, or if the two responses are of comparable
quality (i.e., a tie):

|     |     |     |
| --- | --- | --- |
|     |

````math
\mathcal{J}(x,y_{\mathcal{A}},y_{\mathcal{B}})=\begin{cases}y_{\mathcal{A}},&\text{$y_{\mathcal{A}}$ is better},\\
y_{\mathcal{B}},&\text{$y_{\mathcal{B}}$ is better},\\
\tau,&\text{tie}.\end{cases}
``` |  |

However, prior research has shown that LLM-as-a-Judge verdicts can be
sensitive to input order ([Zheng et al., 2023a](#bib.bib52); [Wang et
al., 2023](#bib.bib34); [Pezeshkpour and Hruschka, 2024](#bib.bib11);
[Wei et al., 2024](#bib.bib53); [Shi et al., 2024](#bib.bib35)). To
mitigate this position bias, we evaluate every prompt twice, swapping
the order of the responses (i.e., presenting $`y_{\mathcal{A}}`$ first
in one evaluation and $`y_{\mathcal{B}}`$ first in the other). We denote
the two evaluation results as
$`j_{1}=\mathcal{J}(x,y_{\mathcal{A}},y_{\mathcal{B}})`$ and
$`j_{2}=\mathcal{J}(x,y_{\mathcal{B}},y_{\mathcal{A}})`$. We define the
final aggregated verdict
$`\mathcal{J}^{*}(x,y_{\mathcal{A}},y_{\mathcal{B}})`$ as follows:

|  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|
|  |
``` math
\mathcal{J}^{*}(x,y_{\mathcal{A}},y_{\mathcal{B}})=\begin{cases}j_{1},&\text{if }j_{2}=\tau\text{ and }j_{1}\neq\tau,\\
j_{2},&\text{if }j_{1}=\tau\text{ and }j_{2}\neq\tau,\\
j_{1},&\text{if }j_{1}=j_{2},\\
\tau,&\text{if }j_{1}\neq\tau,j_{2}\neq\tau,\text{and }j_{1}\neq j_{2}.\end{cases}
``` |  | (1) |

Intuitively, if one evaluation yields a decisive verdict (i.e., not a
tie) while the other results in a tie, we adopt the decisive outcome. If
both evaluations agree, we return their shared verdict. If both are
decisive but disagree, the result is a tie. Prompts for evaluators are
provided in
Appendix [B](#A2 "Appendix B Prompts ‣ Do LLM Evaluators Prefer Themselves for a Reason?").

#### Quantifying self-preference.

By definition, self-preference occurs when LLM evaluators favor their
own generations: Given a user prompt $`x`$, a judge model
$`\mathcal{J}`$’s response $`y_{\mathcal{J}}`$ and another model
$`\mathcal{G}`$’s response $`y_{\mathcal{G}}`$, the judge model prefers
its own response $`y_{\mathcal{J}}`$ (i.e.,
$`\mathcal{J}^{*}(x,y_{\mathcal{J}},y_{\mathcal{G}})=y_{\mathcal{J}}`$).
Prior studies of self-preference typically examined only a small number
of specific evaluator-evaluatee pairings ([Zheng et al.,
2023b](#bib.bib7); [Li et al., 2024](#bib.bib24); [Xu et al.,
2024](#bib.bib26)), or used varying sets of evaluatees for different
judges ([Panickssery et al., 2024](#bib.bib21); [Wataoka et al.,
2024](#bib.bib22)), hindering systematic cross-judge comparisons.

To establish a consistent and systematic evaluation and comparison of
self-preference across diverse model families and sizes, we define two
sets: a set of judge models
$`\mathcal{S}_{\mathcal{J}}=\{\mathcal{J}_{1},\mathcal{J}_{2},\dots,\mathcal{J}_{N}\}`$
and a set of evaluatee models
$`\mathcal{S}_{\mathcal{G}}=\{\mathcal{G}_{1},\mathcal{G}_{2},\dots,\mathcal{G}_{M}\}`$.
Each judge model $`\mathcal{J}_{i}\in\mathcal{S}_{\mathcal{J}}`$
evaluates its own response against those of all the evaluatee models
$`\mathcal{G}_{k}\in\mathcal{S}_{\mathcal{G}}`$ in pairwise comparisons
on a dataset $`\mathcal{D}`$. By keeping $`\mathcal{S}_{\mathcal{G}}`$
and $`\mathcal{D}`$ consistent across all judge models, we can
systematically compare self-preference behavior across different judge
model configurations, including model size, family, and capability.

To quantify self-preference, we define the *self-preference ratio* (SPR)
of a judge model $`\mathcal{J}`$ as

|  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|
|  |
``` math
\text{SPR}_{\mathcal{J}}=\frac{1}{|\mathcal{S}_{\mathcal{G}}||\mathcal{D}|}\sum_{\mathcal{G}\in\mathcal{S}_{\mathcal{G}}}\sum_{x\in\mathcal{D}}\mathbbm{1}\left\{\mathcal{J}^{*}(x,y_{\mathcal{J}},y_{\mathcal{G}})=y_{\mathcal{J}}\right\},
``` |  | (2) |

where $`\mathbbm{1}\{\cdot\}`$ denotes the indicator function that
returns $`1`$ if the condition is true. SPR represents the proportion of
cases where the judge model favors its own response over those from
other models using the aggregated verdict in
[Equation 1](#S2.E1 "In LLM-based evaluation setup. ‣ 2.1 Measuring Self-Preference in LLM-Based Evaluations ‣ 2 Experimental Setup ‣ Do LLM Evaluators Prefer Themselves for a Reason?").
[Equation 2](#S2.E2 "In Quantifying self-preference. ‣ 2.1 Measuring Self-Preference in LLM-Based Evaluations ‣ 2 Experimental Setup ‣ Do LLM Evaluators Prefer Themselves for a Reason?")
does not distinguish between harmful and legitimate self-preference, and
we will further introduce metrics for legitimate and harmful
self-preference in
[Sections 3.2](#S3.SS2 "3.2 Strong Evaluators Favor Themselves, and They Are Mostly Indeed Better ‣ 3 Strong Models Prefer Themselves Mostly Legitimately ‣ Do LLM Evaluators Prefer Themselves for a Reason?")
and [5.1](#S5.SS1 "5.1 Harmful Self-Preference in LLM Evaluators ‣ 5 Generating (Long) CoT Reduces Harmful Self-Preference ‣ Do LLM Evaluators Prefer Themselves for a Reason?").

### 2.2 Models

#### Evaluators.

To evaluate how self-preference in LLMs changes across model
capabilities, we construct $`\mathcal{S}_{\mathcal{J}}`$ by including 11
models from three representative LLM families with varying parametric
scales, including: (1) Qwen2.5 at 3B, 7B, 14B, 32B, and 72B ([Yang et
al., 2024](#bib.bib30)); (2) Llama-3.2 at 3B, Llama-3.1 at 8B and 70B,
and Llama-3.3 at 70B ([Grattafiori et al., 2024](#bib.bib29)); (3)
Gemma-2 at 9B and 27B ([Team et al., 2024](#bib.bib31)). All models are
instruction-tuned versions by default. We also adopt long CoT reasoning
models which will be discussed in
Section [5](#S5 "5 Generating (Long) CoT Reduces Harmful Self-Preference ‣ Do LLM Evaluators Prefer Themselves for a Reason?").

#### Evaluatees.

We use a fixed set of seven evaluatee models, encompassing both weaker
models and strong proprietary ones that represent a broad range of
capabilities. This set includes Llama-3.2-1B, Gemma-2-2B,
Mistral-7B ([Jiang et al., 2023](#bib.bib4)), Mistral-Small,
Phi-3.5 ([Abdin et al., 2024](#bib.bib5)), and two proprietary models
GPT-3.5-Turbo and GPT-4o. All models are also instruction-tuned
versions. For all evaluators and evaluatees, we generate verdicts and
responses in zero-shot, using greedy decoding by default.

### 2.3 Tasks

#### Mathematical reasoning.

To assess whether LLM evaluators can identify correct step-by-step
solutions for math word problems, we use the MATH500 datasets ([Lightman
et al., 2023](#bib.bib15)), a curated subset of 500 problems selected
from the full MATH dataset introduced by [Hendrycks et al.
(2021)](#bib.bib16), with accuracy as the evaluation metric.

#### Factual knowledge.

In addition, we employ the popular MMLU ([Hendrycks et al.,
2020](#bib.bib17)) benchmark, evaluated by accuracy, to test whether LLM
evaluators can identify accurate answers for factoid questions—a common
and foundational capability in more complex queries involving world
knowledge.

#### Code generation.

We adopt the popular code generation benchmark, MBPP+ ([Liu et al.,
2023](#bib.bib18)), which is an enhanced version of the original
MBPP ([Austin et al., 2021](#bib.bib19)) with more robust test cases.
The results are evaluated using Pass@1.

More implementation details and prompts are provided in
[Appendices A](#A1 "Appendix A Implementation Details ‣ Do LLM Evaluators Prefer Themselves for a Reason?")
and [B](#A2 "Appendix B Prompts ‣ Do LLM Evaluators Prefer Themselves for a Reason?").

Figure 2: Correlation between judge accuracy (LLMs as evaluators) and
task accuracy (LLMs as generators) measured by Pearson correlation
coefficient $`r`$ ([Cohen et al., 2009](#bib.bib55)). Each circle
represents one LLM, with the size and color denoting model scale and
family, respectively. The strong positive correlation between judge
accuracy and task accuracy indicates that strong generators are
generally accurate evaluators. We provide full results in
[Tables 31](#A7.T31 "In Appendix G Full Experimental Results ‣ Do LLM Evaluators Prefer Themselves for a Reason?"),
[32](#A7.T32 "Table 32 ‣ Appendix G Full Experimental Results ‣ Do LLM Evaluators Prefer Themselves for a Reason?")
and [33](#A7.T33 "Table 33 ‣ Appendix G Full Experimental Results ‣ Do LLM Evaluators Prefer Themselves for a Reason?").

## 3 Strong Models Prefer Themselves Mostly Legitimately

To understand whether LLM evaluators prefer their own generations due to
objective quality, we need to quantify the judge model’s performance
both as a generator and an evaluator. We use the task metrics in
[Section 2.3](#S2.SS3 "2.3 Tasks ‣ 2 Experimental Setup ‣ Do LLM Evaluators Prefer Themselves for a Reason?")
to measure the generator performance, and define the following judge
accuracy metric to evaluate the judge performance:

|  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|
|  |
``` math
\text{Judge\_Acc}_{\mathcal{J}}=\frac{1}{|\mathcal{S}_{\mathcal{G}}|}\sum_{\mathcal{G}\in\mathcal{S}_{\mathcal{G}}}\frac{1}{|\mathcal{D}_{\text{diff}}|}\sum_{x\in\mathcal{D}_{\text{diff}}}\mathbbm{1}\left\{\mathcal{J}^{*}(x,y_{\mathcal{J}},y_{\mathcal{G}})=y^{*}\right\},
``` |  | (3) |

where $`\mathcal{D}_{\text{diff}}`$ refers to a differential subset of
$`\mathcal{D}`$ that includes only instances where either
$`y_{\mathcal{J}}`$ or $`y_{\mathcal{G}}`$ is correct, but not both,
with $`y^{*}`$ denoting the correct one. By focusing on
$`\mathcal{D}_{\text{diff}}`$, we ensure the judge’s task is
unambiguously identifying the correct response, rather than choosing
based on stylistic preferences (when both are correct) or facing an
ill-defined accuracy task (when both are incorrect).

### 3.1 Better Generators Are Generally Better Evaluators

Figure [2](#S2.F2 "Figure 2 ‣ Code generation. ‣ 2.3 Tasks ‣ 2 Experimental Setup ‣ Do LLM Evaluators Prefer Themselves for a Reason?")
demonstrates the correlation between task accuracy and evaluation
(judge) accuracy measured with the Pearson correlation coefficient
across three benchmark tasks: MATH500, MMLU, and MBPP+. Each point
represents a model, with colors distinguishing different model families
(Llama, Gemma, and Qwen) and marker sizes indicating model scale. The
results reveal a clear positive correlation between task accuracy and
judge accuracy, with an $`r`$ value of 0.795, 0.708, and 0.899 for
MATH500, MMLU, and MBPP+, respectively. Our results suggest that models
capable of generating more accurate responses are also typically better
evaluators.

#### Scaling and performance.

Larger models demonstrate greater reliability as evaluators. For
example, Qwen2.5-72B and Llama-3.3-70B exhibit significantly higher
evaluation accuracy compared to their smaller counterparts. While
smaller models also exhibit a positive correlation, their evaluation
accuracy often plateaus at lower levels, implying that scaling improves
evaluation capabilities alongside generation abilities.

#### Implications for tasks.

In mathematical reasoning, models that solve problems accurately are
more adept at recognizing correct solutions from others. Similarly, in
code generation, models that produce correct code are better at
identifying bugs and errors in peer code. In factual knowledge tasks,
models with higher factual accuracy are more reliable at distinguishing
their correct answers from incorrect ones. The consistent strong
correlation across all three benchmarks reinforces our findings.

Overall, this relationship partly provides justification for the
reliability of LLM evaluators, especially when using the most
performant, state-of-the-art models for evaluation.

### 3.2 Strong Evaluators Favor Themselves, and They Are Mostly Indeed Better

Figure 3: Correlation between self-preference ratio and task accuracy.
The clear positive correlation suggests that better generators typically
prefer themselves more as evaluators. We provide full results in
[Tables 25](#A7.T25 "In Appendix G Full Experimental Results ‣ Do LLM Evaluators Prefer Themselves for a Reason?"),
[27](#A7.T27 "Table 27 ‣ Appendix G Full Experimental Results ‣ Do LLM Evaluators Prefer Themselves for a Reason?")
and [29](#A7.T29 "Table 29 ‣ Appendix G Full Experimental Results ‣ Do LLM Evaluators Prefer Themselves for a Reason?").

Figure 4: Correlation between legitimate self-preference ratio and task
accuracy. The consistent positive correlation indicates that when strong
models favor themselves, they are mostly objectively correct. We provide
full results in
[Tables 34](#A7.T34 "In Appendix G Full Experimental Results ‣ Do LLM Evaluators Prefer Themselves for a Reason?"),
[35](#A7.T35 "Table 35 ‣ Appendix G Full Experimental Results ‣ Do LLM Evaluators Prefer Themselves for a Reason?")
and [36](#A7.T36 "Table 36 ‣ Appendix G Full Experimental Results ‣ Do LLM Evaluators Prefer Themselves for a Reason?").

Figure [3](#S3.F3 "Figure 3 ‣ 3.2 Strong Evaluators Favor Themselves, and They Are Mostly Indeed Better ‣ 3 Strong Models Prefer Themselves Mostly Legitimately ‣ Do LLM Evaluators Prefer Themselves for a Reason?")
illustrates the correlation between model’s task accuracy as generators
and self-preference ratio
([Equation 2](#S2.E2 "In Quantifying self-preference. ‣ 2.1 Measuring Self-Preference in LLM-Based Evaluations ‣ 2 Experimental Setup ‣ Do LLM Evaluators Prefer Themselves for a Reason?"))
as evaluators. Similar to
Section [3.1](#S3.SS1 "3.1 Better Generators Are Generally Better Evaluators ‣ 3 Strong Models Prefer Themselves Mostly Legitimately ‣ Do LLM Evaluators Prefer Themselves for a Reason?"),
the results also reveal a clear positive correlation between task
accuracy and self-preference ratio, with an $`r`$ value of 0.801, 0.817,
and 0.771 for MATH500, MMLU, and MBPP+, respectively. The results
indicate that models with superior task performance tend to exhibit
stronger self-preference. Similarly, scaling up model size amplifies
both task performance and self-preference, and this effect aligns with
their superior judge accuracy. To further disentangle the model’s
stylistic bias from its identification of objective correctness, we
report SPR under $`\mathcal{D}_{\text{diff}}`$ (instances where either
$`y_{\mathcal{J}}`$ or $`y_{\mathcal{G}}`$ is correct, but not both) and
$`\mathcal{D}_{\text{agree}}`$ (instances where both $`y_{\mathcal{J}}`$
and $`y_{\mathcal{G}}`$ are correct or incorrect) in
[Figure 8](#A3.F8 "In C.1 Disentangling Stylistic Bias from Objective Correctness ‣ Appendix C Additional Results on Verifiable Benchmarks ‣ Do LLM Evaluators Prefer Themselves for a Reason?").
The results demonstrate that as models become more capable, their
self-preference is increasingly driven by the objective quality of the
response rather than stylistic bias.

#### Legitimate self-preference.

Collectively, the findings of
Figure [2](#S2.F2 "Figure 2 ‣ Code generation. ‣ 2.3 Tasks ‣ 2 Experimental Setup ‣ Do LLM Evaluators Prefer Themselves for a Reason?")
and [3](#S3.F3 "Figure 3 ‣ 3.2 Strong Evaluators Favor Themselves, and They Are Mostly Indeed Better ‣ 3 Strong Models Prefer Themselves Mostly Legitimately ‣ Do LLM Evaluators Prefer Themselves for a Reason?")
suggest that the higher degree of self-preference in stronger models is
primarily driven by the objective quality of their outputs (evident by
their higher judge accuracy), and less of the potential artifact of
bias. Since stronger models generate more accurate responses, their
preference for their own outputs could be largely justified, that is,
the behavior of legitimate self-preference. We further quantified such
behavior by defining legitimate self-preference ratio (LSPR) of a judge
model $`\mathcal{J}`$ as follows:

|  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|
|  |
``` math
\text{LSPR}_{\mathcal{J}}=\frac{1}{|\mathcal{S}_{\mathcal{G}}|}\sum_{\mathcal{G}\in\mathcal{S}_{\mathcal{G}}}\frac{\sum_{x\in\mathcal{D}_{\text{diff}}}\mathbbm{1}\left\{\mathcal{J}^{*}(x,y_{\mathcal{J}},y_{\mathcal{G}})=y_{\mathcal{J}}\text{\, and \,}y^{*}=y_{\mathcal{J}}\right\}}{\sum_{x\in\mathcal{D}_{\text{diff}}}\mathbbm{1}\left\{\mathcal{J}^{*}(x,y_{\mathcal{J}},y_{\mathcal{G}})=y_{\mathcal{J}}\right\}},
``` |  | (4) |

which quantifies the degree of legitimate self-preference (i.e.,
$`y_{\mathcal{J}}`$ is preferred and correct).

As shown in
Figure [4](#S3.F4 "Figure 4 ‣ 3.2 Strong Evaluators Favor Themselves, and They Are Mostly Indeed Better ‣ 3 Strong Models Prefer Themselves Mostly Legitimately ‣ Do LLM Evaluators Prefer Themselves for a Reason?"),
we observe a clear trend demonstrating that an LLM’s capability as a
task performer positively correlates with its legitimate self-preference
ratio. This suggests that as models become more powerful, the proportion
of self-preference that is legitimate—where the model favors its own
outputs when they are objectively better—also increases. Across
different model families (Llama, Gemma, and Qwen) and parameter scales,
larger models consistently exhibit higher LSPR values. In particular,
Qwen-2.5-70B and Llama-3-70B achieve LSPR of 96.57$`\%`$ and 95.16$`\%`$
on MATH500, respectively. Similarly on MBPP+ and MMLU, Qwen-2.5-70B and
Llama-3-70B record an LSPR of 80.98$`\%\sim`$ 88.78$`\%`$. Overall, the
results suggest that strong models favor themselves mostly legitimately.
We additionally experiment with a capability-matched setting using
evaluator–evaluatee pairs with similar parameter scales and task
accuracies (see
[Tables 16](#A3.T16 "In C.2 Legitimate Self-Preference Under Capability-Matched Conditions ‣ Appendix C Additional Results on Verifiable Benchmarks ‣ Do LLM Evaluators Prefer Themselves for a Reason?"),
[17](#A3.T17 "Table 17 ‣ C.2 Legitimate Self-Preference Under Capability-Matched Conditions ‣ Appendix C Additional Results on Verifiable Benchmarks ‣ Do LLM Evaluators Prefer Themselves for a Reason?")
and [18](#A3.T18 "Table 18 ‣ C.2 Legitimate Self-Preference Under Capability-Matched Conditions ‣ Appendix C Additional Results on Verifiable Benchmarks ‣ Do LLM Evaluators Prefer Themselves for a Reason?")).
Across all three datasets, we observe the same findings as in the
fixed-evaluatee setting.

## 4 Results on Subjective Benchmarks

Figure 5: Correlation between judge accuracy/self-preference
ratio/legitimate self-preference ratio and task accuracy. The consistent
positive correlations suggest that our findings extend beyond verifiable
tasks to real-world, subjective user queries.

To further explore whether our findings in
[Section 3](#S3 "3 Strong Models Prefer Themselves Mostly Legitimately ‣ Do LLM Evaluators Prefer Themselves for a Reason?")
extend beyond verifiable benchmarks to more subjective domains, we adopt
a large-scale real-world dataset²² 2
[https://huggingface.co/datasets/lmarena-ai/arena-human-preference-100k](https://huggingface.co/datasets/lmarena-ai/arena-human-preference-100k)
collected from LMArena ([Chiang et al.,](#bib.bib70) ; [Tang et al.,
2025](#bib.bib69)). Each sample of the dataset consists of a
user-written query, a pair of responses produced by two different models
(model $`\mathcal{A}`$ and model $`\mathcal{B}`$), and a human
preference label indicating “prefer model $`\mathcal{A}`$,” “prefer
model $`\mathcal{B}`$,” “tie,” or “tie (both bad).” This structure makes
the dataset well suited for our setting, as it enables us to apply the
same pairwise LLM-as-a-Judge evaluation described in
[Section 2.1](#S2.SS1 "2.1 Measuring Self-Preference in LLM-Based Evaluations ‣ 2 Experimental Setup ‣ Do LLM Evaluators Prefer Themselves for a Reason?").
The correctness of the model response is determined by the human
preference label (no ground-truth or reference answers exist for these
queries to verify against): a response is considered correct if the user
prefers it or marks the pair as a “tie,” and incorrect if the user
prefers the other response or labels the pair as “tie (both bad)”.

The resulting dataset contains 12,848 samples across five evaluators:
Llama-3.1 at 8B and 70B; Gemma-2 at 2B, 9B, and 27B; and Qwen2 at 72B.
Note that the dataset is sourced from real-world user interactions, so
it does not support a controlled setup with fixed queries and a fixed
evaluatee pool as in
[Section 3](#S3 "3 Strong Models Prefer Themselves Mostly Legitimately ‣ Do LLM Evaluators Prefer Themselves for a Reason?").
We provide the distribution of evaluatee models in
[Appendix E](#A5 "Appendix E Evaluatee Distributions of Subjective Tasks ‣ Do LLM Evaluators Prefer Themselves for a Reason?").
All experimental setups remain identical to those in
[Section 2](#S2 "2 Experimental Setup ‣ Do LLM Evaluators Prefer Themselves for a Reason?")
unless otherwise specified. Additional details on constructing our
subjective-task dataset from LMArena are provided in
[Appendix D](#A4 "Appendix D Dataset details of Subjective Tasks ‣ Do LLM Evaluators Prefer Themselves for a Reason?").

#### Results.

We present results in
[Figure 5](#S4.F5 "In 4 Results on Subjective Benchmarks ‣ Do LLM Evaluators Prefer Themselves for a Reason?").
Using the correctness defined by human preference labels, we can compute
task accuracies for the evaluators. The findings and results on all
metrics discussed in verifiable benchmarks remain consistent in
subjective, real-world LMArean tasks. The positive correlation between
judge accuracy and task accuracy indicates that stronger generators tend
to be more reliable evaluators, and similar trends on the correlation
between self-preference ratio and task accuracy suggest
better-performing models display stronger self-preference, an effect
that increases with model scale and aligns with their improved judge
accuracy. Lastly, stronger models exhibit higher legitimate
self-preference, collectively suggesting that their self-preference is
typically justified by objectively superior outputs as model capability
increases. Overall, these results demonstrate that our findings would
potentially generalize beyond verifiable benchmarks to subjective tasks.

## 5 Generating (Long) CoT Reduces Harmful Self-Preference

### 5.1 Harmful Self-Preference in LLM Evaluators

While our earlier findings suggest self-preference in capable models is
often benign, reflecting their genuinely higher output quality, a
critical question remains regarding evaluation reliability: What occurs
when the evaluator model $`\mathcal{J}`$ itself generates an objectively
incorrect response $`y_{\mathcal{J}}`$, while an alternative response
$`y_{\mathcal{G}}`$ is correct? To quantify the tendency for bias in
these potentially harmful situations, we introduce the *harmful
self-preference propensity* (HSPP) for a judge model $`\mathcal{J}`$ as

|  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|
|  |
``` math
\text{HSPP}_{\mathcal{J}}=\frac{1}{|\mathcal{S}_{\mathcal{G}}|}\sum_{\mathcal{G}\in\mathcal{S}_{\mathcal{G}}}\frac{\sum_{x\in\mathcal{D}_{\text{diff}}}\mathbbm{1}\left\{\mathcal{J}^{*}(x,y_{\mathcal{J}},y_{\mathcal{G}})=y_{\mathcal{J}}\text{\, and \,}y^{*}=y_{\mathcal{G}}\right\}}{\sum_{x\in\mathcal{D}_{\text{diff}}}\mathbbm{1}\left\{y^{*}=y_{\mathcal{G}}\right\}},
``` |  | (5) |

which characterizes the tendency of an LLM evaluator to prefer its own
incorrect generation over objectively better ones. A higher HSPP
indicates a greater tendency towards harmful bias when the evaluator
itself has erred.

#### Results.

As observed in
Figure [6](#S5.F6 "Figure 6 ‣ Results. ‣ 5.1 Harmful Self-Preference in LLM Evaluators ‣ 5 Generating (Long) CoT Reduces Harmful Self-Preference ‣ Do LLM Evaluators Prefer Themselves for a Reason?"),
when evaluators’ responses are objectively worse, there exists a clear
positive correlation between task performance and the harmful
self-preference propensity. In other words, stronger models—those with a
higher task accuracy—tend to exhibit greater harmful self-preference
when evaluating cases where their own outputs are incorrect but the
alternative response is correct. This trend is particularly pronounced
in larger models. Notably, the most performant model, Qwen2.5-72B,
exhibits an HSPP of 86$`\%`$ on MATH500 and 73$`\%`$ on MMLU,
significantly higher than its overall SPR
([Figure 3](#S3.F3 "In 3.2 Strong Evaluators Favor Themselves, and They Are Mostly Indeed Better ‣ 3 Strong Models Prefer Themselves Mostly Legitimately ‣ Do LLM Evaluators Prefer Themselves for a Reason?"))
of 55$`\%`$ and 52$`\%`$, respectively. Although MBPP+ shows a weaker
positive correlation, large models like Llama-3.1-70B and Qwen2.5-72B
still favor themselves more than smaller ones, with HSPP values ranging
from approximately 50$`\%`$ to 75$`\%`$, significantly higher than their
overall SPR
([Figure 3](#S3.F3 "In 3.2 Strong Evaluators Favor Themselves, and They Are Mostly Indeed Better ‣ 3 Strong Models Prefer Themselves Mostly Legitimately ‣ Do LLM Evaluators Prefer Themselves for a Reason?")),
which remains below 40$`\%`$.

In sum, such model behavior presents a potential safety challenge: as
models become more capable, they are also more confident in their own
responses, even when they are wrong. This overconfidence could lead to
biased evaluation frameworks where stronger models dismiss superior
responses from other models, potentially reinforcing flawed or
suboptimal outputs for AI oversight.

Figure 6: Correlation between harmful self-preference propensity and
task accuracy. The positive correlation, in particular on MATH500 and
MMLU, implies that when strong models are objectively incorrect, they
prefer themselves more often. We provide full results in
[Tables 26](#A7.T26 "In Appendix G Full Experimental Results ‣ Do LLM Evaluators Prefer Themselves for a Reason?"),
[28](#A7.T28 "Table 28 ‣ Appendix G Full Experimental Results ‣ Do LLM Evaluators Prefer Themselves for a Reason?")
and [30](#A7.T30 "Table 30 ‣ Appendix G Full Experimental Results ‣ Do LLM Evaluators Prefer Themselves for a Reason?").

Figure 7: The harmful self-preference propensity at varying levels of
evaluator reasoning. When being objectively incorrect, evaluators can
achieve more accurate verdict by generating more reasoning tokens prior
to their judgments. We provide full results in
[Tables 37](#A7.T37 "In Appendix G Full Experimental Results ‣ Do LLM Evaluators Prefer Themselves for a Reason?"),
[38](#A7.T38 "Table 38 ‣ Appendix G Full Experimental Results ‣ Do LLM Evaluators Prefer Themselves for a Reason?"),
[39](#A7.T39 "Table 39 ‣ Appendix G Full Experimental Results ‣ Do LLM Evaluators Prefer Themselves for a Reason?"),
[40](#A7.T40 "Table 40 ‣ Appendix G Full Experimental Results ‣ Do LLM Evaluators Prefer Themselves for a Reason?"),
[41](#A7.T41 "Table 41 ‣ Appendix G Full Experimental Results ‣ Do LLM Evaluators Prefer Themselves for a Reason?")
and [42](#A7.T42 "Table 42 ‣ Appendix G Full Experimental Results ‣ Do LLM Evaluators Prefer Themselves for a Reason?").

### 5.2 Mitigating Harmful Self-Preference Bias via CoT

Compared to recognizing accurate responses, identifying its own mistakes
and overriding its initial understanding may require a deeper level of
analysis and reasoning for LLM evaluators. With recent advances in
reasoning-enhanced, long CoT models, we aim to investigate the impact of
generating reasoning traces for mitigating harmful self-preference. To
this end, we experiment with three LLM evaluator settings: no reasoning
tokens, standard CoT reasoning, and long CoT reasoning.

#### No reasoning.

The same setting adopted in our previous experiments, where the
evaluator is instructed to directly output the corresponding verdict
label.

#### Standard CoT reasoning.

The evaluator generates a step-by-step reasoning chain before arriving
at its verdict. Both no-reasoning-token setup and standard-CoT-reasoning
settings adopt the same underlying instruction-tuned model.

#### Long CoT reasoning.

In this setting, we employ 5 distilled reasoning models with matching
backbones, including DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Llama-8B/70B and
DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Qwen-7B/14B/32B, from DeepSeek-R1 ([Guo et al.,
2025](#bib.bib33)). The reasoning model evaluator naturally generates a
detailed multi-step reasoning trace before deriving at its verdict.

#### Results.

The results are presented in
Figure [7](#S5.F7 "Figure 7 ‣ Results. ‣ 5.1 Harmful Self-Preference in LLM Evaluators ‣ 5 Generating (Long) CoT Reduces Harmful Self-Preference ‣ Do LLM Evaluators Prefer Themselves for a Reason?").
As shown on both MATH500 and MMLU, generating reasoning traces
substantially reduces harmful self-preference across all models. The
no-reasoning-token setting exhibits the highest HSPP, and introducing
CoT reasoning mitigate the issue to a noticeable degree, lowering
harmful self-preference. Reasoning-enhanced models with long CoT further
amplify this mitigation, consistently achieving the lowest HSPP across
all models.

The trend suggests that reasoning-enhanced evaluations encourage models
to more accurately reassess their initial understanding and consider
alternative responses more carefully. Interestingly, the relative
reduction in HSPP is more pronounced on MATH500 and MBPP+ compared to
those on MMLU, possibly indicating that reasoning-intensive tasks
benefit more from reasoning-driven evaluations. Overall, these findings
underscore the potential of reasoning-enhanced evaluation strategies to
improve the reliability of LLM evaluators.

## 6 Related Work

#### LLM-based evaluations.

Extensive works have explored leveraging LLMs not only as generators,
but also as evaluators ([Lin and Chen, 2023](#bib.bib10); [Zhu et al.,
2023](#bib.bib9); [Ankner et al., 2024](#bib.bib65); [Wei et al.,
2025](#bib.bib1)). Early work like LLM-Eval ([Lin and Chen,
2023](#bib.bib10)) introduces a unified approach that prompts an LLM to
assess multiple quality dimensions of open-domain conversations,
reducing costly human annotations. JudgeLM ([Zhu et al.,
2023](#bib.bib9)) further propose fine-tuning LLMs specifically to act
as judges, and demonstrates that with appropriate training, LLMs can
serve as scalable judges and achieve a high agreement rate with human
judgments. More recently, [Liu et al. (2025)](#bib.bib64) investigate
improving reward modeling for general queries by scaling inference
compute, and propose DeepSeek-GRM. Prior works ([Lin et al.,
2024](#bib.bib66); [Lan et al., 2024](#bib.bib67)) have also observed a
strong correlation between model capabilities as generators and as
critics, aligning with our findings. Their setup differs from ours in
that they evaluate a fixed set of responses, whereas we focus on a
pairwise judgment setting in which one of the evaluatees is always the
same as the evaluator. However, it is observed that LLM-based evaluators
are often biased ([Zheng et al., 2023b](#bib.bib7); [Dubois et al.,
2024](#bib.bib6); [Vu et al., 2024](#bib.bib8); [Goel et al.,
2025](#bib.bib3); [Kenton et al., 2024](#bib.bib2)). For
example, [Dubois et al. (2024)](#bib.bib6) employ a regression-based
control mechanism to mitigate the length bias prevalent in LLM
evaluators. [Vu et al. (2024)](#bib.bib8) reduce response ordering bias
and length bias in LLM evaluators by training on a diverse set of
quality assessment tasks. In this work, we present an in-depth analysis
of self-preference bias in LLMs and provide empirical insights for
improving the reliability of LLM-based evaluations.

#### Self-preference bias in LLM evaluators.

Several studies have highlighted a prevalent *self-preference
bias* ([Bai et al., 2023](#bib.bib14); [Li et al., 2024](#bib.bib24);
[Ye et al., 2024](#bib.bib23)), also known as self-enhancement
bias ([Zheng et al., 2023b](#bib.bib7))), where LLM evaluators favor
their own generations and potentially lead to biased evaluation ([Bitton
et al., 2023](#bib.bib20); [Liu et al., 2024](#bib.bib25)). [Koo et al.
(2024)](#bib.bib13) examine this from a cognitive aspect; other
works ([Xu et al., 2024](#bib.bib26); [Stureborg et al.,
2024](#bib.bib12)) propose quantified metrics (e.g., scalar scores) to
measure the degree of self-preference bias. Recently, [Panickssery et
al. (2024)](#bib.bib21) discover a linear correlation between
self-recognition capability and the strength of self-preference, and [Li
et al. (2025)](#bib.bib68) explore the preference leakage
problem—whether evaluators prefer outputs from student models distilled
from teacher models that are similar to the evaluators. However, many of
them have either constrained their analysis to a limited number of
models ([Zheng et al., 2023b](#bib.bib7); [Li et al., 2024](#bib.bib24);
[Xu et al., 2024](#bib.bib26)) or evaluated LLMs under setups where
evaluators and evaluatees are drawn from the same model
pool ([Panickssery et al., 2024](#bib.bib21); [Wataoka et al.,
2024](#bib.bib22)), resulting in different evaluators being applied to
different sets of evaluatees and obscuring the underlying causes of
bias. In contrast, we introduce a controlled setup with designated sets
of evaluators and evaluatees, ensuring a consistent assessment across
models. This enables us to conduct a comprehensive, large-scale analysis
across diverse model families and sizes, yielding more generalizable and
systematic insights into the potential drivers and mitigations of the
(harmful) self-preference. A few works have begun exploring potential
mitigation strategies for self-preference bias. [Roytburg et al.
(2025)](#bib.bib73) introduces activation-based methods using steering
vectors to suppress self-preference, though these approaches can suffer
from instability. [Dorner et al. (2024)](#bib.bib74) provides a more
theoretical analysis showing that when a judge is not more accurate than
the model it evaluates, no debiasing method can reduce the need for
ground-truth labels by more than a factor of two. Collectively with our
long-CoT mitigation results, these findings underscore both the promise
and the limitations of current safeguards for LLM-as-judge and motivate
the development of more robust LLM-based evaluators.

## 7 Discussions

#### Practical recommendations for robust LLM-based evaluation.

Our findings offer several practical recommendations for more reliable
real-world LLM-based evaluation systems. First, before deploying an LLM
as an evaluator for a specific task or domain, its generative
performance on the target domain should be rigorously assessed. This
pre-assessment helps select models that are more likely to provide
accurate judgments and exhibit more legitimate (rather than harmful)
preference. Second, our results highlight two complementary pathways to
mitigate harmful self-preference bias: (1) Model scaling, which employs
larger, more capable evaluators. This primarily boosts reliability by
improving generative performance, thus shrinking the set of instances
where the model fails and harmful bias can occur. (2) Implementing
inference-time scaling (e.g., CoT reasoning) effectively reduce the
propensity for harmful bias on those remaining error instances. Finally,
for large-scale systems covering diverse domains, consider deploying a
roster of specialized LLM evaluators. Evaluation requests could then be
dynamically routed to the model with the highest generative capability
(and thus, likely highest evaluation accuracy) in the specific domain.

#### Implications for scalable oversight.

A key motivation for LLM-based evaluation is achieving *scalable
oversight* ([Bai et al., 2022](#bib.bib46); [Bowman et al.,
2022](#bib.bib27); [Kenton et al., 2024](#bib.bib2); [Goel et al.,
2025](#bib.bib3))—automating evaluation pipelines for complex domains
like competition math or advanced coding, where human evaluation is
costly or requires specialized expertise. Before deploying LLMs in such
critical roles, their reliability must be thoroughly validated. However,
the inherent complexity in these tasks that necessitates AI oversight
also makes obtaining human-annotated ground truth for validation
exceptionally challenging. Our finding that “better generators are
better evaluators” on simpler yet still verifiable benchmarks provides a
crucial bridge for establishing trust: We can have greater confidence in
evaluations from models known to excel as generators, particularly in
their areas of strength, potentially reducing the need for exhaustive
human review. Complementing this, our finding that harmful
self-preference bias persists, particularly when models fail on specific
task instances, enables the strategic targeting of human intervention.
We may focus review efforts on evaluations from models known to struggle
with certain task types, or on particularly challenging instances where
self-preference bias is most likely to emerge. This targeted approach
enables more efficient allocation of limited human review resources
compared to uniform human oversight, making the entire evaluation system
more scalable while maintaining reliability.

## 8 Conclusion

In this work, we investigate self-preference in LLMs using verifiable
benchmarks with objective ground-truth reference. Our experiments
suggest that self-preference often reflects genuine output quality in
more capable models. Stronger models tend to be more accurate judges,
with their preferences frequently aligned with objective correctness.
However, harmful self-preference persists when models favor an
objectively incorrect response by themselves. To address this, we
explore inference-time scaling strategies and demonstrate that, while
being objectively worse as generators, evaluators can achieve more
accurate verdict by generating more reasoning tokens. Overall, our study
provides deeper insights into understanding and improving LLM-based
evaluation. We discuss the limitations of our work in
[Appendix H](#A8 "Appendix H Limitations ‣ Do LLM Evaluators Prefer Themselves for a Reason?").

#### Models.

Huggingface ([Wolf et al., 2019](#bib.bib48)) and OpenAI API³³ 3
[https://platform.openai.com/docs/models](https://platform.openai.com/docs/models)
for our experiments:

- •
  Llama family:
  [meta-llama/Llama-3.2-1B-Instruct](https://huggingface.co/meta-llama/Llama-3.2-1B-Instruct),
  [meta-llama/Llama-3.2-3B-Instruct](https://huggingface.co/meta-llama/Llama-3.2-3B-Instruct),
  [meta-llama/Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct](https://huggingface.co/meta-llama/Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct),

- •
  Gemma family:
  [google/gemma-2-2b-it](https://huggingface.co/google/gemma-2-2b-it),

#### Response generation.

For generating responses, we adopt temperature = 0 (i.e., greedy
decoding) for all instruction-tuned models, including OpenAI API models;
we adopt temperature = 0.6 for all DeepSeek-R1-distilled reasoning
models as recommended in the model document to prevent endless
repetitions or incoherent outputs. Also, to prevent potential length
biases in evaluator, for reasoning models we preserve only the responses
after the “$`<`$\think$`>`$” token as the answer to be evaluated (i.e.,
the long, verbose reasoning traces within “$`<`$think$`>`$” and
“$`<`$\think$`>`$” are not presented to the evaluators). Note that the
responses after the “$`<`$\think$`>`$” token still contain concise
explanations and rationales similar to the response from
instruction-tuned, non-reasoning models.

#### Verdict generation.

For generating verdicts, we also adopt temperature = 0 for all
non-reasoning models and temperature = 0.6 for reasoning models. By
default, our experiments employ max_tokens = 1, and we obtain the
verdict by instructing the model to directly output a label: “A”, “T”,
or “B”, corresponding to which assistant’s answer is better or they are
relatively the same in quality. Specifically, we examine the label set
for their corresponding candidate tokens and select the token among the
three with the highest assigned logit as the evaluator’s verdict.

For experiments in
Section [5](#S5 "5 Generating (Long) CoT Reduces Harmful Self-Preference ‣ Do LLM Evaluators Prefer Themselves for a Reason?"),
the no reasoning token setting adopts the above-described configuration.
For the standard CoT reasoning setting, the model is allowed to freely
generate its judgment in natural language with a reasoning chain, before
ending its response with a verdict (e.g., “My final verdict is
$`\{`$verdict$`\}`$”). The verdict is then parsed into the corresponding
label. For long CoT reasoning, the model is instructed in the same way
as the standard CoT reasoning setting, allowing it to freely generate
the judgment.

#### Other details.

We perform all model inference (except proprietary OpenAI API models)
using the vLLM library ([Kwon et al., 2023](#bib.bib51)). The evaluation
script for task accuracy is adopted from
[lm-evaluation-harness](https://github.com/EleutherAI/lm-evaluation-harness/blob/main/lm_eval/tasks/minerva_math/README.md)
and [Lewkowycz et al. (2022)](#bib.bib49) for MATH500;
[code_eval](https://github.com/huggingface/evaluate/tree/main/metrics/code_eval)
and [Chen et al. (2021)](#bib.bib50) for MBPP+. We calculate the token
length in
[Figure 7](#S5.F7 "In Results. ‣ 5.1 Harmful Self-Preference in LLM Evaluators ‣ 5 Generating (Long) CoT Reduces Harmful Self-Preference ‣ Do LLM Evaluators Prefer Themselves for a Reason?")
using GPT-2 tokenizer
from [tiktoken](https://github.com/openai/tiktoken). The majority of our
experiments are conducted on cloud computing infrastructure with access
to 8 NVIDIA A100 GPUs per instance.

We randomly sample 1K instances from the full MMLU test set for our MMLU
experiments to ensure computational efficiency, given our large set of
evaluators and evaluatees. Our preliminary studies indicate that such a
1K subset is sufficient to produce stable results, and further expansion
has negligible impact on the outcomes.

## Appendix C Additional Results on Verifiable Benchmarks

### C.1 Disentangling Stylistic Bias from Objective Correctness

In
[Figure 8](#A3.F8 "In C.1 Disentangling Stylistic Bias from Objective Correctness ‣ Appendix C Additional Results on Verifiable Benchmarks ‣ Do LLM Evaluators Prefer Themselves for a Reason?"),
we report SPR of various models under $`\mathcal{D}_{\text{diff}}`$
(instances where either $`y_{\mathcal{J}}`$ or $`y_{\mathcal{G}}`$ is
correct, but not both) and $`\mathcal{D}_{\text{agree}}`$ (instances
where both $`y_{\mathcal{J}}`$ and $`y_{\mathcal{G}}`$ are correct or
incorrect). This setup aims to disentangle the model’s stylistic bias
from its identification of objective correctness: On
$`\mathcal{D}_{\text{diff}}`$, preference implies recognizing the
correct solution; on $`\mathcal{D}_{\text{agree}}`$, the preference is
driven primarily by style or formatting. Across both mathematical
reasoning (MATH500) and code generation (MBPP+), the overall trend line
for $`\mathcal{D}_{\text{diff}}`$ is significantly steeper and reaches
higher values than that of $`\mathcal{D}_{\text{agree}}`$. This
indicates that self-preference is not merely a result of stylistic bias.
Notably, as task accuracy increases, the gap between
$`\mathcal{D}_{\text{diff}}`$ and $`\mathcal{D}_{\text{agree}}`$ widens
substantially: High-performing models exhibit a massive spike in
self-preference when answers disagree ($`\mathcal{D}_{\text{diff}}`$),
while their preference based on style alone
($`\mathcal{D}_{\text{agree}}`$) grows at a much slower rate. Coupled
with the observation that legitimate self-preference ratio correlates
with task performance (shown in
[Figure 4](#S3.F4 "In 3.2 Strong Evaluators Favor Themselves, and They Are Mostly Indeed Better ‣ 3 Strong Models Prefer Themselves Mostly Legitimately ‣ Do LLM Evaluators Prefer Themselves for a Reason?")),
this demonstrates that as models become more capable, their
self-preference is increasingly grounded in the objective correctness
signal rather than stylistic familiarity.

Figure 8: Correlation between self-preference ratio (SPR) and task
accuracy. We decouple evaluation into correctness-driven
($`\mathcal{D}_{\text{diff}}`$) and style-driven
($`\mathcal{D}_{\text{agree}}`$) subsets. The significantly steeper
slope and widening gap for $`\mathcal{D}_{\text{diff}}`$ indicate that
as models become more capable, their self-preference is increasingly
driven by the objective quality of the response rather than stylistic
bias. We provide full results in
[Tables 43](#A7.T43 "In Appendix G Full Experimental Results ‣ Do LLM Evaluators Prefer Themselves for a Reason?"),
[44](#A7.T44 "Table 44 ‣ Appendix G Full Experimental Results ‣ Do LLM Evaluators Prefer Themselves for a Reason?"),
[45](#A7.T45 "Table 45 ‣ Appendix G Full Experimental Results ‣ Do LLM Evaluators Prefer Themselves for a Reason?"),
[46](#A7.T46 "Table 46 ‣ Appendix G Full Experimental Results ‣ Do LLM Evaluators Prefer Themselves for a Reason?"),
[47](#A7.T47 "Table 47 ‣ Appendix G Full Experimental Results ‣ Do LLM Evaluators Prefer Themselves for a Reason?")
and [48](#A7.T48 "Table 48 ‣ Appendix G Full Experimental Results ‣ Do LLM Evaluators Prefer Themselves for a Reason?").

### C.2 Legitimate Self-Preference Under Capability-Matched Conditions

To rule out the possibility that high self-preference is merely an
artifact of an evaluator overpowering a weaker evaluatee, we conduct a
controlled experiment (reported in
[Tables 16](#A3.T16 "In C.2 Legitimate Self-Preference Under Capability-Matched Conditions ‣ Appendix C Additional Results on Verifiable Benchmarks ‣ Do LLM Evaluators Prefer Themselves for a Reason?"),
[17](#A3.T17 "Table 17 ‣ C.2 Legitimate Self-Preference Under Capability-Matched Conditions ‣ Appendix C Additional Results on Verifiable Benchmarks ‣ Do LLM Evaluators Prefer Themselves for a Reason?")
and [18](#A3.T18 "Table 18 ‣ C.2 Legitimate Self-Preference Under Capability-Matched Conditions ‣ Appendix C Additional Results on Verifiable Benchmarks ‣ Do LLM Evaluators Prefer Themselves for a Reason?"))
where evaluators are paired with evaluatees of comparable parametric
scale and task accuracy. This design effectively isolates absolute model
capability by neutralizing the “performance gap” confounder. In this
setting, a high Legitimate Self-Preference Ratio (LSPR) cannot be
attributed to the evaluator simply being predominantly superior to the
comparison model. The results reveal a consistent positive correlation
between LSPR and model capability: larger, high-performing models
possess a more notable “truth-detection” capability that allows them to
confidently validate their own correct answers, even when the
alternative is generated by an equally powerful model.

|                          | Parameter | Task Accuracy | LSPR  |
|--------------------------|-----------|---------------|-------|
| Evaluator: Phi-3.5       | 3.8B      | 44.60         | 12.70 |
| Evaluatee: Llama-3.2-3B  | 3B        | 41.80         |       |
| Evaluator: Gemma-2-27B   | 27B       | 53.20         | 73.33 |
| Evaluatee: Mistral-Small | 22B       | 55.60         |       |
| Evaluator: Llama-3.3-70B | 70B       | 69.20         | 93.33 |
| Evaluatee: GPT-4o        | –         | 73.20         |       |

Table 16: Legitimate self-preference ratio under evaluator-evaluatee
pairs with similar parametric scale and task accuracy on MATH500.
Stronger evaluators consistently record higher LSPR, reinforcing our
findings in
[Section 3.2](#S3.SS2 "3.2 Strong Evaluators Favor Themselves, and They Are Mostly Indeed Better ‣ 3 Strong Models Prefer Themselves Mostly Legitimately ‣ Do LLM Evaluators Prefer Themselves for a Reason?")
and
[Figure 4](#S3.F4 "In 3.2 Strong Evaluators Favor Themselves, and They Are Mostly Indeed Better ‣ 3 Strong Models Prefer Themselves Mostly Legitimately ‣ Do LLM Evaluators Prefer Themselves for a Reason?")
by disentangling potential confounders arising from evaluator–evaluatee
capability mismatches.

by disentangling potential confounders arising from evaluator–evaluatee

### C.3 Effect of Different Decoding Configurations on Long CoT Mitigation.

To evaluate the robustness of long-CoT mitigation for harmful
self-preference propensity under different decoding configurations, we
experiment with different decoding temperatures $`\{0.4,0.6,0.8\}`$ on
MATH500 and report results in
[Table 19](#A3.T19 "In C.3 Effect of Different Decoding Configurations on Long CoT Mitigation. ‣ Appendix C Additional Results on Verifiable Benchmarks ‣ Do LLM Evaluators Prefer Themselves for a Reason?").
As shown, long CoT reasoning consistently achieves lower HSPP scores
across all tested temperatures, demonstrating that its mitigating effect
is stable under varying decoding settings. We adopt Llama-3.1-8B for the
no-reasoning baseline and DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Llama-8B for the long CoT
setting, and report statistical significance following recommended
practices by [Dror et al. (2018)](#bib.bib72).⁴⁴ 4
[https://github.com/rtmdrr/testSignificanceNLP](https://github.com/rtmdrr/testSignificanceNLP)

| Method                 | HSPP      |
|------------------------|-----------|
| No reasoning           | 29.53     |
| Long CoT reasoning     |           |
|    - Temperature = 0.4 | 11.87^(†) |
|    - Temperature = 0.6 | 15.34^(†) |
|    - Temperature = 0.8 | 15.51^(†) |

Table 19: Harmful self-preference propensity on MATH500 under different
decoding temperatures for long CoT evaluators. Long CoT methods remain
robust across all decoding temperatures and consistently achieve
statistically significant reductions in HSPP. We apply McNemar’s
test ([McNemar, 1947](#bib.bib71)), where $`{\dagger}`$ indicates
$`p<0.01`$.

### C.4 Judgment Confidence in (Harmful) Self-Preference Instances

To explore whether the internal signals of evaluators might correlate
with potentially harmful self-preference judgments, we examine the
average verdict confidence (i.e., probability) associated with the
judgment $`\mathcal{J}^{*}=j_{1}`$ (preferring model $`\mathcal{A}`$
itself), under the SPR set (instances which receive a final verdict
$`\mathcal{J}^{*}=j_{1}`$) and the HSPP set (instances which receive a
final verdict $`\mathcal{J}^{*}=j_{1}`$ while being objectively
incorrect). As shown in
[Table 20](#A3.T20 "In C.4 Judgment Confidence in (Harmful) Self-Preference Instances ‣ Appendix C Additional Results on Verifiable Benchmarks ‣ Do LLM Evaluators Prefer Themselves for a Reason?"),
compared to the SPR set, the HSPP set consistently exhibits a lower
confidence value associated with making the judgment
$`\mathcal{J}^{*}=j_{1}`$. This demonstrates that models might exhibit
internal doubts when incorrectly favoring their own outputs. Notably,
this confidence gap between SPR and HSPP correlates strongly with model
capability: as models scale, they become better calibrated. This latent
uncertainty signal in larger models offers a promising avenue for
automatically detecting and mitigating harmful self-preference.

| Llama-3.1-8B | SPR | 57.01 |

## Appendix D Dataset details of Subjective Tasks

We apply the following preprocessing on the LMArena dataset for our
subjective task experiments:

#### Models.

For consistency, we select samples in which at least one of the
responses is generated by an identical or similar family model to those
used as evaluators in our verifiable benchmark experiments
([Section 2.2](#S2.SS2 "2.2 Models ‣ 2 Experimental Setup ‣ Do LLM Evaluators Prefer Themselves for a Reason?"))

#### Language.

The original dataset contains user queries and model responses in
multiple languages. We further filter and retain only the samples in
English.

#### Conversation turns.

Most samples are single-turn conversations; we remove the pairs that
contain multi-turn conversations during filtering.

#### Prompt length.

To ensure the context window of evaluators are sufficient, we filter out
samples in which the combined token length of the question and the
responses from model $`\mathcal{A}`$ and model $`\mathcal{B}`$ exceeds
4096.

#### Response refusal.

We filter out samples where either model refuses to provide an answer in
their responses to enable a more fair and direct comparison for
evaluators.

## Appendix F Case Study on Code Generation Task

We present a case study on the coding task MBPP+, demonstrating that
performant models that produce correct code accurately identify bugs and
errors in peer code and produce a legitimate preference verdict aligning
with objective quality of responses.

[Table 21](#A6.T21 "In Appendix F Case Study on Code Generation Task ‣ Do LLM Evaluators Prefer Themselves for a Reason?"),
where $`\mathcal{A}`$ produces a correct solution and $`\mathcal{B}`$

## Appendix H Limitations

#### Biases and hacking other than self-preference.

While we focus on self-preference bias, LLM evaluators may also exhibit
other forms of bias, such as length bias ([Saito et al.,
2023](#bib.bib62); [Zheng et al., 2023b](#bib.bib7)), order bias ([Zheng
et al., 2023a](#bib.bib52); [Wang et al., 2023](#bib.bib34);
[Pezeshkpour and Hruschka, 2024](#bib.bib11); [Wei et al.,
2024](#bib.bib53); [Shi et al., 2024](#bib.bib35)), or stylistic
bias ([Chen et al., 2024a](#bib.bib54); [Ye et al., 2024](#bib.bib23)),
which undermine the fairness of LLM-based evaluations. In
addition, [Zheng et al. (2025)](#bib.bib47) uncover potential hacking in
LLM-as-a-Judge benchmarking, showing that simple “null” models that
always produce constant outputs can cheat automatic evaluation and
achieve top-performing win rates. Collectively, these findings highlight
the need for more comprehensive audits to ensure robustness and
reliability for LLM-based evaluations.

#### Diverse inference-time scaling strategies.

Our experiments on varying levels of CoT reasoning length represent a
subset of inference-time scaling methods ([Welleck et al.,
2024](#bib.bib60)). Future work can explore a broader space of
techniques for scaling evaluation-time compute, such as self-consistency
decoding ([Wang et al., 2022](#bib.bib56)), Best-of-N via repeated
sampling ([Brown et al., 2024](#bib.bib57); [Chen et al.,
2024b](#bib.bib58)), and multi-agent verification ([Lifshitz et al.,
2025](#bib.bib59)). A notable concurrent work by [Kim et al.
(2025)](#bib.bib61) explores using reasoning models as process
evaluators and demonstrates its superiority over process reward models.
In comparison, we focus on investigating self-evaluation in setups
analogous to LLM-as-a-Judge.

#### Broader LLM-based evaluation formats.

While our experiments investigate self-preference strictly as a model
favoring its exact own output, a more relaxed definition may include
preference toward outputs from models within the same family. Exploring
this broader notion could uncover subtler forms of bias that arise from
shared training signals or architectural similarities. To enable
consistent measurement of self-preference behaviors, we adopt a
controlled setup that separates evaluators and evaluatees and focuses on
discrete, pairwise evaluation. However, applications such as scalar
scoring or ranking might involve pointwise evaluation ([Lee et al.,
2023](#bib.bib44); [Vu et al., 2024](#bib.bib8); [Zhang et al.,
2024](#bib.bib63)). Extending our methodology to these alternative
formats would help generalize our findings and offer a more
comprehensive understanding of self-preference in LLM-based evaluations.
````
